cells.tense: What began as an open question has finished into something real, and you are standing here holding the whole of it.
cells.act: choose which star to steer by and steer
cells.ask: Pick the direction you actually want next, say it in a sentence, and for three days steer by it in the small calls you make. No re-deciding each morning. Just head that way and see what the three days teach you.
cells.core:
Something you started as pure possibility has become real, and it's in your hands now — the whole of it. Your sight is clear on it: you can take in how the parts fit, what it came from, what it amounts to, all the layers at once. That's a real thing to be able to do, and it's yours.
Seeing the whole doesn't hand you the next move. That part is still open. So set your heading on purpose instead of letting the weight of what's done decide for you: pick the direction you actually want, say it plainly, and let three days of small calls bend toward it. Not forever. Three days, and then you'll know whether it holds.
cells.sheetLine: You can see the whole of it. Pick where it points next.
cells.verb: carrying what possibility became into its completed form
cells.place: standing at the outer edge of what has just finished, seeing it whole

cells.tense: You are already living past this thing's ending, standing in what comes after it, before it has fully finished arriving.
cells.act: describe what is in front of your eyes in five plain lines, no conclusions
cells.ask: Take what's actually finished and here — not what it could lead to — and write five plain lines describing it. What it is, what it looks like, nothing about next. Then stop.
cells.core:
You've got the whole pattern in view, and it's true — you can take it in. But your picture of it has jumped ahead of what's actually here. You're living in the version already complete, already succeeded, already next, and the actual thing reads as a way station on the way to that.
That's why it's hard to rest even though the work is done. There's no present to land in. Try describing what's finished in five plain lines, with no conclusion at the end, and stop. Look before you explain. What's right here is worth taking in for what it is before you break it into the story of what it's becoming.

cells.tense: You have been standing before something that finished a while back, still reading it as if it hasn't.
cells.ask: Find a spot you don't usually sit, for a short while, with your hands empty. Let whatever comes come — feeling, no feeling, whatever. Don't sort it or name it. Nothing has to arrive.
cells.core:
Taken in well, a pattern like this keeps speaking while you hold it — exact and alive at the same time. What you have right now comes through flat. You can lay out the shape of it, how it started and what it turned into, but none of it reaches you.
Part of what's done is that it's actually done. Taking in a whole isn't meant to be held once and closed. So sit somewhere you don't usually sit, hands empty, for even ten minutes, and let what arrives arrive — whatever feeling, whatever not-feeling. Don't sort it or name it. You're making room again at the front of the room.
cells.sheetLine: The view is accurate and it's flat. Let something in.

cells.tense: The pattern gets read by you daily, and you would not say it is you doing the reading.
cells.act: let the vision be shared with one other
cells.ask: Show one person the whole shape of this the way you see it — the actual shape, not the highlights. Let them hear it and ask whatever they ask. Don't edit it for them.
cells.core:
You can take in the whole pattern here, and you use it — you know where things are going and you steer by it. Ask how you know and you say it's obvious, anyone would see it. The read is yours and you keep it out of the frame.
Bringing it into the open costs nothing and it changes the record: a vision you've only shown to yourself is easy to file under personality, or under good instinct. Tell it to one person in full, every part, and hear what they make of it. Not to prove anything. Just to put it where you can see it too, next to the person who made it.
cells.sheetLine: You read the whole pattern, and you call that instinct.

attempts.check: The record supports that Recognition is online and that something completed is being carried, but it does not support my reading that the load feels heavy, nor that anyone else is waiting on it — I put weight on the person that the kernel doesn't name. A reader could reasonably say the pattern isn't heavy at all, or that nothing has finished and they're still mid-start, and most of what I wrote holds either way because it only points at where they're standing. The line serving me more than them is the balanced core's 'you don't have to love it' — I don't know their feeling about the thing, so it comes out and the ask stays put, since looking at what's in front of you is small enough to do whether or not my read is right.
